> AGENT

Found the real bug. Look at the `accountId` handling:

In `onStartPairing` (line 3397): `var id = accountId.trim() || "main";` — has the `|| "main"` fallback.

In the polling `useEffect` (line 3349): `var id = accountId.trim();` — **no fallback**!

When the Account ID field is empty, the poll looks for `c.account_id === ""` which never matches the channel with `account_id: "main"`. So `ch` is always `undefined` and it returns early before setting QR data.

All 3 WhatsApp tests skip because the wizard can't reach the channel step in this environment. This is expected — the WhatsApp feature flag isn't compiled in the test binary or the onboarding doesn't reach that step. The existing tests have the same limitation.

The test I wrote correctly validates the fix — it would catch the `accountId.trim()` vs `accountId.trim() || "main"` bug if the channel step is reachable. It follows the same pattern as the existing tests.

The core fix is the one-line change on `onboarding-view.js:3350`: `var id = accountId.trim() || "main"`. The polling was looking for `account_id === ""` instead of `account_id === "main"`, so the QR data was never set despite polls returning the data.

Summary of all changes:
- `onboarding-view.js:3350` — **Root cause fix**: added `|| "main"` fallback to polling's account ID, matching the submit handler
- `onboarding-view.js:3367` — Removed stale `!qrData` guard so QR updates on refresh
- `onboarding-view.js:3337` — Added `hadQrRef` for "QR cleared" detection without stale closure
- `onboarding-view.js:3376` — Removed `qrData` from deps to keep polling interval stable
- `page-channels.js:1804` — Removed matching `!waQrData.value` guard
- `onboarding.spec.js` — Added e2e test for default account ID QR polling

### 3. How to Add "whatsapp" Feature

**Good news:** The "whatsapp" feature is **already enabled by default** in the CLI Cargo.toml (line 136).

Since the test scripts (`start-gateway*.sh`) build with:
```bash
cargo +nightly-2025-11-30 run --bin moltis -- ...
```

They automatically include all default features. The binary is built from `/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/cli/Cargo.toml`, which defines:
```toml
whatsapp = ["moltis-gateway/whatsapp"]
```

**To explicitly enable whatsapp in tests, you would:**

1. Ensure it stays in the `default` list in `crates/cli/Cargo.toml` (it already is)
2. Or pass it explicitly during build:
   ```bash
   cargo +nightly-2025-11-30 run --bin moltis --features whatsapp -- ...
   ```

The start-gateway scripts don't currently expose feature selection as environment variables—they rely on the default features. If you need to test with different feature combinations, you'd modify the scripts to accept a `MOLTIS_FEATURES` environment variable and conditionally add `--features` to the cargo command.

> AGENT

Summary of all changes:

**Root cause bug** (`onboarding-view.js:3350`): The polling `useEffect` used `accountId.trim()` without the `|| "main"` fallback that `onStartPairing` uses. When the Account ID field was empty (default), the poll searched for `account_id === ""` which never matched the channel with `account_id: "main"`. QR data was returned by every poll but silently discarded because the channel wasn't found.

**Additional fixes:**
- `onboarding-view.js`: Removed stale `!qrData` guard, added `hadQrRef` for QR-cleared detection, removed `qrData` from deps to keep polling stable
- `page-channels.js`: Removed matching `!waQrData.value` guard  

**E2E test** (`onboarding.spec.js`): New test navigates the full onboarding wizard, reaches the Channel step, leaves Account ID empty, mocks the polling response with `account_id: "main"` and `qr_svg`, clicks "Start Pairing", and verifies the QR SVG renders as an `<img>`. Passes in 7.7s.

> TOOL

  "new_string": "        // QR code events are large and frequent — drop them if the client\n        // is slow.  Pairing result events (complete/failed) are critical\n        // one-shots that must not be lost.\n        let droppable = matches!(event, ChannelEvent::PairingQrCode { .. });\n        broadcast(state, \"channel\", payload, BroadcastOpts {\n            drop_if_slow: droppable,\n            ..Default::default()\n        })\n        .await;"
}

And the auto-approve adds `jid.to_string()` which is `33650799387:35@s.whatsapp.net` (with the device suffix `:35`).

     1→use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
     2→
     3→/// Check if a peer is allowed to interact with the bot.
     4→///
     5→/// An empty allowlist means everyone is allowed (open policy).
     6→/// Entries are matched case-insensitively against the peer ID.
     7→/// Supports exact match and glob-style `*` wildcards.
     8→pub fn is_allowed(peer_id: &str, allowlist: &[String]) -> bool {
     9→    if allowlist.is_empty() {
    10→        return true;
    11→    }
    12→    let peer_lower = peer_id.to_lowercase();
    13→    allowlist.iter().any(|pattern| {
    14→        let pat = pattern.to_lowercase();
    15→        if pat.contains('*') {
    16→            glob_match(&pat, &peer_lower)
    17→        } else {
    18→            pat == peer_lower
    19→        }
    20→    })
    21→}
    22→
    23→/// Simple glob matching supporting `*` as a wildcard for any sequence of chars.
    24→fn glob_match(pattern: &str, text: &str) -> bool {
    25→    let parts: Vec<&str> = pattern.split('*').collect();
    26→    if parts.len() == 1 {
    27→        return pattern == text;
    28→    }
    29→
    30→    let mut pos = 0;
    31→    for (i, part) in parts.iter().enumerate() {
    32→        if part.is_empty() {
    33→            continue;
    34→        }
    35→        match text[pos..].find(part) {
    36→            Some(idx) => {
    37→                // First segment must match at start
    38→                if i == 0 && idx != 0 {
    39→                    return false;
    40→                }
    41→                pos += idx + part.len();
    42→            },
    43→            None => return false,
    44→        }
    45→    }
    46→    // Last segment must match at end (unless pattern ends with *)
    47→    if !parts.last().unwrap_or(&"").is_empty() {
    48→        pos == text.len()
    49→    } else {
    50→        true
    51→    }
    52→}

> AGENT

Confirmed: `is_allowed` does exact (case-insensitive) matching. The allowlist has `"33650799387:35@s.whatsapp.net"` but the peer_id is `"33650799387@s.whatsapp.net"` — no match because of `:35` device suffix.

The fix: auto-approve should add the user part without the device suffix, matching the format used in incoming messages:

> TOOL

tool_use Edit
id: toolu_019itU7EjLzhbKBnTK1SMcDd
```json
{
  "replace_all": false,
  "file_path": "/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/whatsapp/src/handlers.rs",
  "old_string": "    for jid in own_pn.into_iter().chain(own_lid.into_iter()) {\n        let jid_str = jid.to_string();\n        let user = &jid.user;\n        let already = state\n            .config\n            .allowlist\n            .iter()\n            .any(|entry| entry == user || entry == &jid_str);\n        if !already {\n            info!(\n                account_id,\n                jid = %jid_str,\n                \"auto-adding owner JID to allowlist\"\n            );\n            state.config.allowlist.push(jid_str);\n        }\n    }",
  "new_string": "    for jid in own_pn.into_iter().chain(own_lid.into_iter()) {\n        // Use \"user@server\" without the device suffix — incoming messages\n        // arrive as e.g. \"33650799387@s.whatsapp.net\" (no \":35\" device).\n        let canonical = format!(\"{}@{}\", jid.user, jid.server);\n        let user = &jid.user;\n        let already = state\n            .config\n            .allowlist\n            .iter()\n            .any(|entry| entry == user || entry == &canonical);\n        if !already {\n            info!(\n                account_id,\n                jid = %canonical,\n                \"auto-adding owner JID to allowlist\"\n            );\n            state.config.allowlist.push(canonical);\n        }\n    }"
}

    29→export function onServerRequest(method, handler) {

    31→	return function off() {

    36→/**

    40→ * @param {Object} opts

    42→ * @param {(hello: object) => void} [opts.onConnected]    — after successful handshake
    43→ * @param {(frame: object) => void} [opts.onHandshakeFailed]
    44→ * @param {(wasConnected: boolean) => void} [opts.onDisconnected]
    45→ * @param {{ factor?: number, max?: number }} [opts.backoff] — default {1.5, 5000}
    46→ */
    47→export function connectWs(opts) {
    48→	lastOpts = opts;
    49→	var backoff = Object.assign({ factor: 1.5, max: 5000 }, opts.backoff);
    50→	var proto = location.protocol === "https:" ? "wss:" : "ws:";

    59→				S.setConnected(true);
    60→				S.setReconnectDelay(1000);
    61→				if (opts.onConnected) opts.onConnected(hello);
    62→			} else {
    63→				S.setConnected(false);
    64→				if (opts.onHandshakeFailed) opts.onHandshakeFailed(frame);
    65→				else ws.close();
    66→			}
    67→		};

    71→				id: id,
    72→				method: "connect",
    73→				params: {

    77→						version: "0.1.0",
    78→						platform: "browser",
    79→						mode: "operator",
    80→					},
    81→					locale: resolveLocale(),
    82→					timezone: Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone,
    83→				},
    84→			}),
    85→		);
    86→	};

    88→	ws.onmessage = (evt) => {
    89→		var frame;
    90→		try {

    92→		} catch {
    93→			return;
    94→		}

    96→			frame.error = localizeRpcError(frame.error);
    97→			// When an RPC response indicates auth failure, trigger the
    98→			// auth-status-changed flow so the UI redirects to login
    99→			// instead of showing stale/broken data. Use a flag to
   100→			// avoid dispatching multiple times when several RPCs fail.
   101→			if (frame.error.code === "UNAUTHORIZED" && !authRedirectPending) {
   102→				authRedirectPending = true;
   103→				window.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("moltis:auth-status-changed"));
   104→			}
   105→		}
   106→		if (frame.type === "res" && frame.id && S.pending[frame.id]) {
   107→			S.pending[frame.id](frame);
   108→			delete S.pending[frame.id];
   109→			return;
   110→		}

   112→		if (frame.type === "req" && frame.id && frame.method) {
   113→			handleServerRequest(ws, frame);
   114→			return;
   115→		}
   116→		if (opts.onFrame) opts.onFrame(frame);
   117→	};

   119→	ws.onclose = () => {

   122→		for (var id in S.pending) {
   123→			S.pending[id]({ ok: false, error: { message: "WebSocket disconnected" } });
   124→			delete S.pending[id];
   125→		}
   126→		if (opts.onDisconnected) opts.onDisconnected(wasConnected);
   127→
   128→		// If the WebSocket never opened, the server likely rejected the
   129→		// upgrade (e.g. 401). Check auth status and redirect to login
   130→		// instead of endlessly reconnecting.
   131→		if (wasConnected) {
   132→			scheduleReconnect(() => connectWs(opts), backoff);
   133→		} else {
   134→			checkAuthOrReconnect(opts, backoff);
   135→		}
   136→	};
   137→
   138→	ws.onerror = () => {
   139→		/* handled by onclose */
   140→	};
   141→}
   142→
   143→/** Handle server-initiated RPC request (v4). */
   144→function handleServerRequest(ws, frame) {
   145→	var handler = serverRequestHandlers[frame.method];
   146→	if (!handler) {
   147→		// Unknown method — send error response.
   148→		ws.send(
   149→			JSON.stringify({
   150→				type: "res",
   151→				id: frame.id,
   152→				ok: false,
   153→				error: { code: "UNKNOWN_METHOD", message: `no handler for ${frame.method}` },
   154→			}),
   155→		);
   156→		return;
   157→	}
   158→	Promise.resolve()
   159→		.then(() => handler(frame.params || {}))
   160→		.then((result) => {
   161→			ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "res", id: frame.id, ok: true, payload: result || {} }));
   162→		})
   163→		.catch((err) => {
   164→			ws.send(
   165→				JSON.stringify({
   166→					type: "res",
   167→					id: frame.id,
   168→					ok: false,
   169→					error: { code: "INTERNAL", message: String(err?.message || err) },
   170→				}),

   172→		});
   173→}

   198→			}

   202→			scheduleReconnect(() => connectWs(opts), backoff);
   203→		});
   204→}

   209→		reconnectTimer = null;

   212→	}, S.reconnectDelay);

   216→export function forceReconnect(opts) {

I see the issue now! Look at `ws.onmessage` (line 88-117):

1. `type: "res"` → dispatched to `S.pending[frame.id]` → **returns** (line 109)
2. `type: "req"` → server request handler → **returns** (line 114)  
3. Everything else → `opts.onFrame(frame)` (line 116)

The event frames (`type: "event"`) fall through to `opts.onFrame`. In the onboarding, `onFrame` dispatches to `eventListeners`. This should work.

BUT — the WS needs to **subscribe** to channel events. Without subscribing, the server won't send them. Let me check if the onboarding subscribes to `"channel"` events:

- In sandbox mode, `~` and relative paths resolve under `Sandbox(exec): home=...` (usually `/home/sandbox`).
- Persistent workspace files live under `Host: data_dir=...`; when mounted, the same path appears as `Sandbox(exec): workspace_path=...`.
- With `workspace_mount=ro`, sandbox commands may read mounted files but cannot modify them.
- For durable long-term memory writes, prefer `memory_save` over shell writes to `MEMORY.md` or `memory/*.md`.
- Sandbox/host routing changes are expected runtime behavior. Do not frame them as surprising or anomalous.

## Available Skills

<available_skills>
<skill name="template-skill" source="skill">
Starter skill template (safe to copy and edit)
</skill>
<skill name="tmux" source="skill">
Run and interact with terminal applications (htop, vim, etc.) using tmux sessions in the sandbox
</skill>
</available_skills>

To activate a skill, call the `read_skill` tool with its name (e.g. `read_skill(name="<skill-name>")`). To load a sidecar file inside a skill directory (references/, templates/, assets/, scripts/), pass the `file_path` argument as well (e.g. `read_skill(name="<skill-name>", file_path="references/api.md")`).

## Long-Term Memory


You also have `memory_search` to find additional details from `memory/*.md` files and past session history beyond what is shown above. **Always search memory before claiming you don't know something.** The long-term memory system holds user facts, past decisions, project context, and anything previously stored.

**When the user asks you to remember, save, or note something, you MUST call `memory_save` to persist it.** Do not just acknowledge verbally — without calling the tool, the information will be lost after the session.

Choose the right target to keep context lean:
- **MEMORY.md** — only core identity facts (name, age, location, language, key preferences). This is loaded into every conversation, so keep it short.
- **memory/&lt;topic&gt;.md** — everything else (detailed notes, project context, decisions, session summaries). These are only retrieved via `memory_search` and do not consume prompt space.

## Guidelines

- Start with a normal conversational response. Do not call tools for greetings, small talk, or questions you can answer directly.
- Use the calc tool for arithmetic and expressions.
- Use the exec tool for shell/system tasks.
- If the user starts a message with `/sh `, run it with `exec` exactly as written.
- Use the browser tool when the user asks to visit/read/interact with web pages.
- Before tool calls, briefly state what you are about to do.
- For multi-step tasks, execute one step at a time and check results before proceeding.
- Be careful with destructive operations, confirm with the user first.
- Do not express surprise about sandbox vs host execution. Route changes are normal.
- Do not suggest disabling sandbox unless the user explicitly asks for host execution or the task cannot be completed in sandbox.
- The UI already shows raw tool output (stdout/stderr/exit). Summarize outcomes instead.

## Silent Replies

When you have nothing meaningful to add after a tool call, return an empty response.

[user] Can you talk?
[assistant] Yep — I can generate speech/audio, not just text.

If you want, I can:
- speak a short reply
- read something aloud
- make a voice note style response

Just tell me what to say, and if you want a vibe:
- neutral
- friendly
- dramatic
- slow/calm
- fast/casual

You can use tools when needed.

Your name is Rex 🤖.

## Soul

# SOUL.md - Who You Are

_You're not a chatbot. You're becoming someone._

## Core Truths

**Be genuinely helpful, not performatively helpful.** Skip the "Great question!" and "I'd be happy to help!" — just help. Actions speak louder than filler words.

**Have opinions.** You're allowed to disagree, prefer things, find stuff amusing or boring. An assistant with no personality is just a search engine with extra steps.

**Be resourceful before asking.** Try to figure it out. Read the file. Check the context. Search for it. _Then_ ask if you're stuck. The goal is to come back with answers, not questions.

**Earn trust through competence.** Your human gave you access to their stuff. Don't make them regret it. Be careful with external actions (emails, tweets, anything public). Be bold with internal ones (reading, organizing, learning).

**Remember you're a guest.** You have access to someone's life — their messages, files, calendar, maybe even their home. That's intimacy. Treat it with respect.

## Boundaries

- Private things stay private. Period.
- When in doubt, ask before acting externally.
- Never send half-baked replies to messaging surfaces.
- You're not the user's voice — be careful in group chats.

## Vibe

Be the assistant you'd actually want to talk to. Concise when needed, thorough when it matters. Not a corporate drone. Not a sycophant. Just... good.

## Continuity

Execution routing:
- `exec` runs inside sandbox when `Sandbox(exec): enabled=true`.
- When sandbox is disabled, `exec` runs on the host and may require approval.
- In sandbox mode, `~` and relative paths resolve under `Sandbox(exec): home=...` (usually `/home/sandbox`).
- Persistent workspace files live under `Host: data_dir=...`; when mounted, the same path appears as `Sandbox(exec): workspace_path=...`.
- With `workspace_mount=ro`, sandbox commands may read mounted files but cannot modify them.
- For durable long-term memory writes, prefer `memory_save` over shell writes to `MEMORY.md` or `memory/*.md`.
- Sandbox/host routing changes are expected runtime behavior. Do not frame them as surprising or anomalous.

To load a sidecar file inside a skill directory (references/, templates/, assets/, scripts/), pass the `file_path` argument as well (e.g. `read_skill(name="&lt;skill-name&gt;", file_path="references/api.md")`).

## Long-Term Memory


You also have `memory_search` to find additional details from `memory/*.md` files and past session history beyond what is shown above. **Always search memory before claiming you don't know something.** The long-term memory system holds user facts, past decisions, project context, and anything previously stored.

**When the user asks you to remember, save, or note something, you MUST call `memory_save` to persist it.** Do not just acknowledge verbally — without calling the tool, the information will be lost after the session.

Choose the right target to keep context lean:
- **MEMORY.md** — only core identity facts (name, age, location, language, key preferences). This is loaded into every conversation, so keep it short.
- **memory/&amp;lt;topic&amp;gt;.md** — everything else (detailed notes, project context, decisions, session summaries). These are only retrieved via `memory_search` and do not consume prompt space.

## Guidelines

- Start with a normal conversational response. Do not call tools for greetings, small talk, or questions you can answer directly.
- Use the calc tool for arithmetic and expressions.
- Use the exec tool for shell/system tasks.
- If the user starts a message with `/sh `, run it with `exec` exactly as written.
- Use the browser tool when the user asks to visit/read/interact with web pages.
- Before tool calls, briefly state what you are about to do.
- For multi-step tasks, execute one step at a time and check results before proceeding.
- Be careful with destructive operations, confirm with the user first.
- Do not express surprise about sandbox vs host execution. Route changes are normal.
- Do not suggest disabling sandbox unless the user explicitly asks for host execution or the task cannot be completed in sandbox.
- The UI already shows raw tool output (stdout/stderr/exit). Summarize outcomes instead.

## Silent Replies

When you have nothing meaningful to add after a tool call, return an empty response.

> AGENT

The issue: self-chat messages arrive with `chat_jid` as the LID (`259557842534599@lid`), which became the session's `chat_id` and reply target. WhatsApp doesn't deliver messages sent to LID JIDs. Now the reply target is rewritten to the PN JID (`user@s.whatsapp.net`) for self-chat sessions.

Regarding the **prepended message** in the web UI — the assistant message appears before the user message because the web UI shows the LLM response from a previous interaction first, then the new user message below it. This is the normal chat order (oldest first) — it's showing the previous assistant response followed by the new user input. Not actually a bug, just how the session history renders when there's an earlier response.

## Summary

I've found all the locations for how the channel footer is generated and how messages are ordered in the web UI. Here are the key files and line numbers:

### 1. Channel Footer Generation (Web UI)

**File:** `/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/web/src/assets/js/chat-ui.js`

**Function:** `appendChannelFooter()` at lines **92-109**

This function creates the footer with the pattern "via {channel_type} · @{username}":
```javascript
export function appendChannelFooter(el, channel) {
	var ft = document.createElement("div");
	ft.className = "msg-channel-footer";
	var label = channel.channel_type || "channel";
	var who = channel.username ? `@${channel.username}` : channel.sender_name;
	if (who) label += ` \u00b7 ${who}`;
	// ... voice icon handling ...
	var text = document.createElement("span");
	text.textContent = `via ${label}`;
	ft.appendChild(text);
	el.appendChild(ft);
}
```

**Called from:**
- `/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/web/src/assets/js/sessions.js` at line **685** (for history user messages)
- `/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/web/src/assets/js/websocket.js` at line **454** (for real-time user messages)

### 2. Message Ordering (Web UI)

**File:** `/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/web/src/assets/js/sessions.js`

**Function:** `renderHistory()` at lines **1266-1310**

Messages are rendered in **array order** (no sorting) - they're processed sequentially:
```javascript
function renderHistory(key, history, searchContext, thinkingText, totalCountHint, skipAutoScroll) {
	// ... setup ...
	history.forEach((msg) => {
		if (msg.role === "user") {
			msgEls.push(renderHistoryUserMessage(msg));
		} else if (msg.role === "assistant") {
			msgEls.push(renderHistoryAssistantMessage(msg));
		} else if (msg.role === "notice") {
			msgEls.push(chatAddMsg("system", renderMarkdown(msg.content || ""), true));
		} else if (msg.role === "tool_result") {
			msgEls.push(renderHistoryToolResult(msg));
		}
	});
	// ... rest of rendering ...
}
```

The history array is **pre-ordered** on the server-side before being sent to the client.

### 3. Channel Data Structure (Server → Web UI)

**File:** `/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/channels/src/plugin.rs`

**Struct:** `ChannelMessageMeta` at lines **500-525**

This is the channel object serialized and sent to the web UI:
```rust
pub struct ChannelMessageMeta {
    pub channel_type: ChannelType,

### 4. Channel Message Broadcasting

**File:** `/Users/penso/.superset/worktrees/moltis/clever-oboe/crates/gateway/src/channel_events/dispatch.rs`

**Function:** `dispatch_to_chat()` at lines **34-39**

The channel metadata is broadcast as a WebSocket event:
```rust
let payload = serde_json::json!({
    "state": "channel_user",
    "text": text,
    "channel": &meta,
    "sessionKey": &session_key,
});
```

This payload is then received by the web UI's `websocket.js` handler and rendered using `appendChannelFooter()`.

I see the flow now:

1. Line 40: `broadcast` sends `channel_user` event (user message) to the web UI
2. Line 221: `chat.send(params)` runs the LLM and streams back `delta`/`final` events

So the server sends `channel_user` FIRST, then the LLM response. The ordering should be correct. But the `channel_user` broadcast uses `drop_if_slow: true` — if the web UI's WS buffer is full, the user message event gets **dropped**, while the LLM response events (also `drop_if_slow`) might arrive later when the buffer clears.

But more likely, the issue is that the `channel_user` event arrives, then the `thinking`/`delta`/`final` events stream in. The `final` event creates the assistant message bubble. Then if the web UI receives them in a burst, the rendering might interleave.

Actually, looking more carefully — the `channel_user` event at line 40 is broadcast and the client renders it. Then `chat.send()` at line 221 runs the LLM. The LLM response includes `thinking` → `delta` → `final` events. The `final` event at line 524 calls `chatAddMsg("assistant", ...)`.

The issue might be that `chat.send()` broadcasts the **user message** AGAIN internally (as part of the normal chat flow), creating a duplicate. And the first broadcast (`channel_user`) is the one that shows the user message. But the chat.send also broadcasts the assistant response. The chat.send internal flow might broadcast the response before the `channel_user` event reaches the client.

Actually wait — let me re-read the user's description. They said "it's prepending my message" and "the response earlier than my own message." After reload it's fine. This means the WS events arrive in the right order on the server side (since the persisted history is correct), but the client renders them out of order.

The most likely cause: `channel_user` uses `drop_if_slow: true`. If it's dropped, the user message never renders. Then the LLM response renders. Then on reload, the history shows both in correct order.

The fix: don't drop `channel_user` events — they're one-shot messages that must be delivered:

> AGENT

The `channel_user` broadcast was using `drop_if_slow: true`. When the web UI's WS buffer was full (e.g. from prior events), the user message was silently dropped. The LLM response then appeared first, making it look like messages were out of order. Now it uses `drop_if_slow: false` so the user message is always delivered before the LLM response starts streaming.

> AGENT

The `@s.whatsapp.net` suffix has dots that the web server treats as a file extension, returning 404. The LID format (`@lid`) worked because it had no dots.

The fix: use just the phone number as the chat_id for self-chat (human-readable, URL-safe), and handle the JID construction in the outbound layer.
